title: Industrial Networking: Modbus & Deterministic Polling
oneLiner: How does a PLC actually talk to an HMI (human-machine interface: the operator's screen), a SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition) system that monitors a whole site, or another PLC? Usually with a protocol built around one machine ASKING and another ANSWERING, not the general internet's anyone-can-initiate model.
keyTakeaway: Modbus (and most classic industrial protocols) are MASTER-SLAVE: the master (often an HMI or SCADA system) always initiates every request, and a slave device (a PLC) only ever responds when asked -- deterministic polling, not the general internet's model where either side can send a request whenever it wants (see TCP vs UDP, DNS & HTTP for that model).
explanation:
Modbus is one of the oldest and still most common industrial protocols, originally designed for serial connections (Modbus RTU) and later adapted to run over Ethernet (Modbus TCP) -- and its core model has stayed the same the whole time: a MASTER (often an HMI, a SCADA system, or a higher-level PLC) sends a request, and a SLAVE (often a PLC, an I/O module, or a sensor) only ever responds when directly asked. There's no equivalent of a web server pushing an update to a browser unprompted (see DNS & HTTP for that model) -- if the master doesn't poll a register, nothing gets sent, period. That's DETERMINISTIC POLLING: the master decides exactly what gets read, in what order, how often, which trades responsiveness (nothing arrives faster than the polling cycle) for exactly the kind of predictability PLCs need everywhere else (see PLCs: How They're Different From a Normal Computer's scan cycle for the same theme).

The data itself is organized into numbered REGISTERS (and, for on/off values, COILS) -- a slave device exposes a fixed table of registers, and a master reads or writes them by address and function code (Read Holding Registers, Write Single Coil, etc.). Because classic Modbus registers are just 16-bit integers, values that aren't naturally whole numbers get SCALED -- a temperature of 72.5°F might be transmitted as the raw integer 725, with both sides agreeing to divide by 10 -- a real, still-common workaround for protocols designed before floating-point values were assumed, and a classic source of an off-by-a-factor-of-10 bug if the scaling isn't applied consistently on both ends.

EtherNet/IP (the IP stands for Industrial Protocol) and other modern fieldbus protocols add more capability on top (faster cycle times, richer data types, built-in device discovery) but keep the same fundamental shape -- a controller exchanging data with field devices on a fixed cycle (EtherNet/IP uses producer/consumer connections rather than Modbus-style polling), layered on top of the same OSI/TCP-IP stack covered in Networking (Modbus TCP, for instance, is just Modbus's request/response messages carried inside ordinary TCP segments on port 502).
